understandingReviews.editorialFinding: Distinguished replication from transcription and supplied accurate basic terms.
Removed duplicate pairing explanation while retaining semi-conservative inheritance and fidelity limits.
Clarified helicase vs polymerase with non-repeated causal mechanism.
Separated PCR amplification from size-based electrophoresis and strengthened definitions.
Removed duplicate profiling caveats and explained reliability of multiple markers.
Identified the free 3′-OH chemical reason for 5′→3′ synthesis.
Explained opposite synthesis geometry and primer requirement on lagging DNA.
Specified four distinct enzymes in the syllabus-limited prokaryotic model.
Identified mismatched 3′ nucleotide removal by polymerase III proofreading.
Distinguished dendrites, axon and cell body; summarized membrane voltage signalling.
Separated gradient maintenance by ATP pump from the K⁺ permeability that generates negative resting voltage.
Clarified action potential as propagated ion-driven voltage signal, not electron flow.
Explained different mechanisms for conduction speed: axon resistance and myelin.
Distinguished polarized release site, cleft and postsynaptic receptors.
Sequenced arrival → calcium influx → exocytosis and distinguished calcium from transmitter.
Linked acetylcholine-receptor activation to an excitatory postsynaptic potential.
Defined threshold, Na⁺ depolarization and K⁺ repolarization.
Explained regeneration by local currents and refractory unidirectionality.
Clarified interpreting time-voltage traces and converting spike count to Hz.
Linked myelin current insulation to node-specific spike regeneration.
Distinguished receptor disruption by neonicotinoids from reuptake inhibition by cocaine.
Centered IB-specified hyperpolarization and firing inhibition.
Clarified spatial/temporal summation and all-or-nothing outcome.
Distinguished nociceptor transduction from conscious pain processing.
Explained emergence of consciousness at network rather than cell level.
Distinguished cell-like vesicles from inheriting, selectable protocell lineages without claiming a known origin pathway.
Distinguished catalytic-RNA evidence from the unresolved evolutionary RNA-world hypothesis.
Explained evaporative tension and causal effect of stomatal closure; corrected root pump misconception.
Replaced tautological summary with source–sink pressure-flow mechanism and leaf–fruit example.
Defined three modes of selection via reproductive success and clarified curves versus proof.
Removed duplicate numerical working; stated recessive-phenotype assumptions before q² calculation.

patches.originalValue:
The two parental DNA strands separate. Each becomes a template for synthesis of a complementary new strand, producing two double helices that each contain one original strand and one newly made strand. This arrangement is called semi-conservative, not conservative or dispersive.

A pairs with T and G pairs with C in DNA. When a template exposes a base, the matching incoming deoxyribonucleotide can pair at that position. Enzyme selectivity and later proofreading further increase fidelity: complementary pairing alone is not an absolute guarantee against mistakes.

A template strand does not dictate where its own bases remain; it determines the order of incoming complementary nucleotides. Separating the two parental strands therefore produces two templates, each leading to one parental-plus-new double helix. A pairs with T and G with C. The rule strongly supports accuracy but does not make errors impossible.

patches.originalValue:
Helicase uses energy to unwind the parental double helix and disrupt the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, exposing the two template strands. The sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact at the fork; helicase does not cut the strands into nucleotides.

DNA polymerase selects incoming deoxyribonucleotides against the DNA template and catalyses phosphodiester-bond formation in the growing strand. In ordinary cellular replication it extends an existing primer rather than starting a strand from nothing. Its accuracy depends on base selection and, for proofreading polymerases, exonuclease activity.

Helicase disrupts hydrogen bonds between paired bases without cutting the sugar–phosphate backbone. Exposed parental strands are templates; DNA polymerase selects matching DNA nucleotides and makes covalent phosphodiester links in the growing daughter chain. Helicase and polymerase carry out different chemical tasks.

In cellular replication it extends a pre-existing 3′ end rather than starting synthesis from nothing. Helicase separates the strands; polymerase builds their complementary copies.

patches.originalValue:
A PCR cycle first heats DNA to separate strands, then lowers the temperature so short DNA primers can anneal to complementary sequences on opposite strands, then allows thermostable Taq DNA polymerase to extend those primers. The chosen primers define the target; repeated cycles can produce many copies of the region. PCR is not the same as replication of an entire chromosome.

Negatively charged DNA migrates toward the positive electrode through a gel under an electric field. Under comparable conditions, shorter DNA fragments generally travel farther through the gel. DNA ladders supply reference fragment lengths; a band position is evidence about fragment size, not by itself the complete nucleotide sequence.

Temperature makes three different things possible in successive PCR stages: high heat separates template strands, cooling allows short primers to anneal to flanking complementary sites, and extension at the polymerase's working temperature copies the bounded region. Taq polymerase is heat-stable. In agarose gel electrophoresis, negatively charged DNA migrates toward the positive electrode; with an appropriate gel and conditions, smaller fragments generally travel farther.

DNA has a negatively charged sugar–phosphate backbone, so an electric field draws fragments toward the positive electrode. patches.originalValue:
Forensic investigations and parentage testing compare informative DNA markers. Amplification makes small samples analysable and gel or capillary separation distinguishes fragment-length patterns. Agreement at one marker is weak evidence; combining multiple independent markers can greatly reduce the chance of a coincidental match.

A DNA profile is evidence to be interpreted with sample integrity, contamination controls, population frequencies and a documented chain of custody. A match does not prove when or how biological material arrived at a scene, nor does a paternity result identify a person using one band alone.

A matching DNA-band or STR profile is evidence of consistency with a sample source, not a proof that excludes contamination, relatives or procedural error. More independently selected markers usually decrease the probability of a coincidental match. Interpretation depends on sample handling, population frequencies, and a defensible statistical model; biological relatedness complicates paternity and forensic comparisons.
patches.proposedReplacement:

A DNA-marker match is evidence that two samples may share a source, not certainty about identity. Multiple independent markers reduce coincidental matches, but contamination, close relatives, population frequencies and sample handling still matter to a forensic or parentage conclusion.

A DNA strand has chemically different 5′ and 3′ ends because nucleotides have a phosphate-linked 5′ carbon and a hydroxyl-bearing 3′ carbon. The two template strands in a duplex run antiparallel. DNA polymerase attaches an incoming nucleotide's 5′ phosphate to the free 3′ hydroxyl of the growing strand; every new DNA strand therefore elongates 5′→3′.

As polymerase extends new DNA in the 5′→3′ direction, it reads the complementary template in the 3′→5′ direction. An arrow in a diagram must identify whether it shows fork motion, template direction or strand elongation; these are not interchangeable.

The phosphate of an incoming dNTP attaches to the free 3′-OH of the nascent chain, so elongation is always 5′→3′. Polymerase reads its template antiparallel, 3′→5′. Mark both directions separately on a diagram; reversing the fork direction changes which template is leading, never the chemical direction of polymerization.

On the leading-strand template, a newly primed strand is extended continuously in the same overall direction in which the replication fork opens. Because the polymerase can only extend a 3′ end, the leading template is read 3′→5′ toward the fork.

The opposing lagging template has the reverse polarity, so short RNA primers must be placed repeatedly on newly exposed DNA. Each Okazaki fragment is extended 5′→3′ away from the advancing fork. Fragment synthesis is discontinuous, even though the finished lagging daughter strand becomes one continuous DNA molecule after primer replacement and ligation.

At a fork travelling right, a 3′→5′ template oriented left-to-right can be copied toward the fork continuously; its opposing 5′→3′ template needs repeated primers and short fragments made away from the fork. Okazaki fragments are eventually joined into a continuous daughter molecule. Both strands still elongate 5′→3′.

The opposite template polarity requires repeated RNA primers on the lagging strand. Each Okazaki fragment still grows 5′→3′, but away from the advancing fork; the RNA primers are later replaced and ligase joins the fragments. The leading strand instead grows continuously toward the fork after its initial primer.

patches.originalValue:
In the prokaryotic system specified by the guide, primase makes short RNA primers that provide the free 3′ end needed by DNA polymerase III. Polymerase III extends the DNA segment while reading the parental template. Leading synthesis typically needs one initiation at a fork; lagging synthesis needs a fresh primer for each fragment.

DNA polymerase I removes RNA primers and replaces them with DNA. DNA ligase then seals remaining nicks in the sugar–phosphate backbone, creating continuous DNA. The enzyme numbers refer to bacterial polymerases; do not automatically transplant this division of labour to eukaryotic replication.

In the prokaryotic model required here, primase synthesizes RNA primers because polymerases need an existing 3′-OH. DNA polymerase III extends the primers with DNA, polymerase I removes RNA primer nucleotides and replaces them with DNA, and ligase seals remaining nicks between adjacent DNA fragments. patches.originalValue:
Water evaporates from moist mesophyll walls and leaves through stomata. The removal lowers local water potential and pulls replacement water from adjacent cell walls and xylem. The resulting tension (negative pressure potential) is transmitted downward through the xylem's cohesive column.

Hydrogen bonding supplies cohesion between water molecules, preventing the stretched column from fragmenting under ordinary conditions. Adhesion and capillary interactions help wet narrow walls and transfer water through cell-wall spaces, but evaporation-generated tension is the main driver of high-tree transport. No transpiration-powered pump is located at the roots. The transpiration stream is largely a passive physical process within dead xylem vessels; energy expenditure elsewhere in the plant does not constitute a xylem pump.

A high, sunlit tree can move water upward without an ATP-powered xylem pump. Evaporation in leaves generates tension that pulls a continuous cohesive xylem column.

patches.originalValue:
Mature sieve tube elements form long living conduits with perforated sieve plates, very reduced cytoplasm and organelles, and no nucleus. Their companion cells retain nuclei, many mitochondria and abundant plasmodesmata connecting to sieve elements.

ATP-dependent loading of sucrose at a source raises osmotic concentration, encouraging water entry from xylem and raising turgor pressure. Phloem sap flows by bulk mass flow toward lower-pressure sinks, where solutes are unloaded for use or storage. The direction of a given sieve tube depends on source–sink relations, not simply gravity. Sucrose can move toward different sinks in different sieve tubes; a plant does not have one universal upward or downward phloem direction.

Growing fruits are strong phloem sinks while mature photosynthesizing leaves are common sources. Living sieve elements and metabolically active companion cells support pressure-flow translocation.

For two alleles A and a, define p as frequency of A and q as frequency of a: p+q=1. Under the Hardy–Weinberg random-mating model, genotype frequencies are p² (AA), 2pq (Aa) and q² (aa), summing to 1.

If an appropriate fully penetrant recessive phenotype occurs with frequency 0.09, then q²=0.09, q=0.30, p=0.70 and expected heterozygotes are 2pq=0.42 (42%). The square root is nonnegative. This model predicts population proportions only when assumptions are defensible; it does not specify exact outcomes in each family.

If recessive phenotype frequency q² = 0.09, assuming Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, q = 0.30 and p = 0.70. Expected heterozygote frequency 2pq = 2 × 0.70 × 0.30 = 0.42 or 42%. q² is a genotype frequency, whereas q is an allele frequency; the two cannot be interchanged.
patches.proposedReplacement:
For two alleles A and a, define p as frequency of A and q as frequency of a: p+q=1. Under the Hardy–Weinberg random-mating model, genotype frequencies are p² (AA), 2pq (Aa) and q² (aa), summing to 1.

A recessive phenotype can estimate q² only if the trait is caused by the relevant fully penetrant recessive genotype and the Hardy–Weinberg model is appropriate. First estimate q² from the phenotype frequency, then take its nonnegative square root to obtain q; p = 1 − q. Dominant phenotype counts cannot, on their own, separate AA from Aa.

Suppose 9% of a suitable population shows the recessive aa phenotype. Under Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, q² = 0.09, so q = √0.09 = 0.30 and p = 1 − 0.30 = 0.70. The predicted heterozygote frequency is 2pq = 2 × 0.70 × 0.30 = 0.42 (42%). q is an allele frequency, not the fraction of individuals with aa.
